intro/what-is-papertrade.title: What is Papertrade?
intro/what-is-papertrade.lead: Papertrade is a fair-launched, fully on-chain perpetuals exchange built on Hyperliquid, with several unique features:
intro/what-is-papertrade.text:
1000× leverage 
 One-click Buy/Sell, no orderbook 
 Zero slippage 
 No funding costs 
 Self-bootstrapping LP 
 No funding costs or spread 
 

 How it runs 
 Papertrade's smart contract uses Hyperliquid's BBO mid as an oracle to create synthetic swaps between the user and the LP. No perpetual contracts are traded on Hyperliquid itself. The contract lives on the HyperEVM L1 and reads HyperCore state through precompiles. 
 papertrade.xyz is the first canonical frontend for the protocol, built to make the initial trading experience seamless and responsive. 

 How trades work 
 All trades on Papertrade are synthetic swaps between the user and the LP: no orderbook, no matching engine, no other counterparty. When you open a position, the contract reads Hyperliquid's BBO mid through a precompile and locks that price as your entry. When you close, the contract reads BBO mid again and settles PnL directly against the LP. 
 Because no actual perpetual contract changes hands on Hyperliquid, there are no funding costs. There is also no slippage: you get the BBO mid regardless of size, subject to per-instrument OI safety caps. 

 The LP and PAPER 
 The LP bootstraps itself from zero using the Martingaler Protocol. All trades face the LP directly, and the LP grows over time from cumulative user losses. If the LP goes insolvent, it issues debt into a queue, which pays out as soon as the LP receives funds from another user's loss. 
 Trading while the LP is low or insolvent is incentivised: PAPER mints fastest in that regime, and the queue pays out automatically as future losses refill the LP. 
 PAPER is the LP fee-claim token, minted from realised user losses. There is no way to deposit directly into the LP; the only path to exposure is through trade losses that mint PAPER for you. PAPER is a fair launch : supply starts at zero, with no pre-mint, no team allocation, no VC allocation, no airdrop, and no vesting. Every token in existence has to be minted through the on-chain emissions curve. The launch profile makes PAPER non-transferable except for staking and unstaking. The mint rate is flat at 100 PAPER per $1 of loss mint basis while tracked LP is below $2M (including underwater), then decays asymptotically past that point. 
 Staked PAPER earns USDC from two sources, both flowing from the LP, never from the user. (1) A share of LP revenue: every settlement that credits the LP carves a small slice for stakers continuously. The user pays nothing extra; this is a cut of the LP's revenue, not a trading fee. (2) LP excess sweep: once the LP balance climbs above the $5M staker reward cap , every dollar of further LP gain past that point is fully distributable to stakers via the keeper's pushStakerFees() call. Below $5M, stakers only receive the LP-revenue share. 

 No conventional trading fee 
 Papertrade has no notional swap fee, no spread, and no funding cost. At 1000× leverage, none of those would scale sustainably. Instead, the protocol applies an asymmetric impact on profitable closes and LP-side fee carves on solvent settlements. Losses pay nothing on top of the loss itself.

martingaler/overview.title: Martingaler LP
martingaler/overview.lead: How Papertrade's LP bootstraps from zero with no upfront capital. A summary of the relevant parts of the Martin Galer whitepaper.
martingaler/overview.text:
Why this mechanism 
 Papertrade's LP is built on the Martingaler mechanism, designed to launch an asynchronous speculation game with no upfront LP capital and no constraints on bet size. The full whitepaper walks through the theory; this page captures the parts directly relevant to Papertrade. 
 Traditional onchain speculation games (SatoshiDice, Bustabit, Etheroll, EtherCrash) all needed an LP pool seeded upfront. That meant either centralised capital (with all the trust and incentive design that entails) or token rewards that complicated the protocol's economics. EtherCrash famously had its LP drained by a bad actor; Rollbit-style platforms still face the same solvency anxiety from users. 
 The Martingaler mechanism removes both constraints (no initial LP, no bet-size cap) by replacing instant-payout LP economics with a payout queue. 

 The payout queue 
 Instead of holding an LP that pays winners on demand, the protocol routes every winning wager through a FIFO queue. The protocol can be temporarily insolvent on aggregate, but every winner gets paid in order as soon as solvency permits. 
 Per-wager logic: 
 
 A new wager is placed and wins. 
 If a queue already exists:
 
 Add the wager to the back of the queue. 
 Evaluate whether the front of the queue can now be paid out (per the solvency ratio). 
 If yes, pay it out. 
 
 
 If no queue exists:
 
 Evaluate whether this wager can be paid out directly. 
 If yes, pay it. Otherwise, start a queue of length one with this wager. 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 The queue absorbs variance that an LP couldn't have absorbed on its own. Multiple front-of-queue payouts can fire per new wager when solvency allows. In Papertrade's deployed accounting, losses go to treasury while the queue is empty; while the queue is active they park in sideBucket so they can be harvested into queued payouts without temporarily inflating LP solvency. 

 Why token emissions help 
 Token emissions let a positive-house-edge game present as +EV for the player by remunerating realised losses with a claim on future protocol value. Early participants, who carry the most variance risk, are rewarded most. 
 For Papertrade, this is implemented as the PAPER mint curve : 100 tokens per dollar of loss mint basis while tracked LP is below $2M (the flat region, including underwater), then decaying asymptotically past that point. The flat-region rate is what makes early trading attractive even before the LP becomes solvent. 

 Whitepaper 
 Full text: A Bootstrapping Mechanism for Sustainable Asynchronous Speculation Games of Chance (Galer). 
 The whitepaper also covers worked examples (a fair coin flip; a 3/4-chance-to-win-4/3 game with positive house edge), a yield-bearing-collateral variant, and a queue-redemption escape valve for stuck participants. Those are out of scope for Papertrade as deployed; this page summarises only the parts that map to the live system.

intro/faq.title: FAQ
intro/faq.lead: Common questions about how Papertrade works, what it costs, and what's actually onchain.
intro/faq.text:
How is it onchain? 
 All of Papertrade's trading logic lives entirely on the HyperEVM L1 (Hyperliquid's smart-contract layer), while USDC balances are held entirely on HyperCore (Hyperliquid's native spot ledger). The two are kept separate: the Exchange contract on HyperEVM tracks all trading state (positions, queue, per-user balances) and moves USDC through HyperCore via CoreWriter precompile actions. 
 For the gated trading surface, public maintenance paths, and admin-key model see Risk . 

 How do trades work? 
 Trades are synthetic swaps between the user and the LP. No perpetual contracts are traded on Hyperliquid. Each trade executes at Hyperliquid's order-book mid. No funding costs and no slippage: you get the BBO mid regardless of size, subject to the per-instrument OI cap. 
 When you first connect, the app creates a session key for you, which eliminates the need to confirm future trades with a wallet signature. 

 How does the oracle work? 
 Papertrade reads prices through Hyperliquid precompiles : a free, instant, reliable oracle that any HyperEVM contract can read directly from within the L1. No off-chain feed, no signer, no admin key. 

 What markets are available, and what's the max leverage? 
 Currently BTC and ETH , both with up to 1000× leverage and a per-user position cap of $10M . The protocol can list any perpetual contract on Hyperliquid, including HIP-3 markets. New markets are added by the contract owner via the timelock. 

 What does it cost to trade? 
 In order to maintain solvency given the trader-favoured nature of offering no slippage at BBO, the protocol uses three fee/impact mechanics over the long term: 
 
 Asymmetric impact on profitable closes: a smooth haircut on the closing PnL that scales with how far price moved between entry and exit. Losses pay nothing on top of the loss itself. 
 A 0.2 bps jitter-protection fee applied at execution (see Risk for details). 
 A small LP-side staking/dev carve routed from solvent settlement proceeds, not charged on top of a user's loss (see Staking & claims ). 
 

 Can I add margin to my position? 
 No. Every position is a discrete slug that cannot be modified once opened. If you want more headroom on a position, close it and reopen with more margin. 

 What happens during a liquidation? 
 Each position has a displayed bust price , which is deliberately set a small distance before the voluntary close path would exhaust the position's equity. Liquidation is a hard bust: crossing the displayed bust price forfeits the full isolated margin, even if a voluntary close immediately beforehand could return some equity. Once the BBO crosses that trigger, any keeper can call liquidate(positionId) ; the contract removes the position and applies the full-margin liquidation accounting. 
 Liquidations are run by an open keeper script; anyone can run one. The protocol team operates a keeper but doesn't have exclusive access to the function. 

 Is PAPER fairly launched? 
 Yes. PAPER starts from a supply of zero . There is no pre-mint, no team allocation, no VC allocation, no airdrop, and no vesting schedule. Every token in existence has been minted to a trader who closed at a loss or got liquidated. The supply is purely community-owned by definition: the only mint path is through trading. In the relayer-only launch profile, arbitrary PAPER transfers are disabled; staking and unstaking still work. 

 How can I deposit to the LP? 
 You can't. The LP is made of cumulative user losses, and the PAPER token owns the future LP revenue. The only way to earn PAPER is to close a losing trade, which directly adds to the LP and mints PAPER for you. If you already hold PAPER, you can stake it to start earning the staker share of LP revenue, paid in USDC. 

 Can I build my own frontend? 
 Yes, but the launch profile is relayer-gated for trading. Third-party frontends can integrate by producing the same signed intents and submitting them through the authorised relayer/batcher path. Direct public trading entrypoints exist in the open and session-fee contract profiles, but the relayer-only deployment restricts opens, closes, session-key registration, proxy deployment, and staking actions to configured executors. Withdrawals still require the user's real wallet signature, and liquidations/harvest-style maintenance remain open.

intro/quick-start.title: Quick start
intro/quick-start.text:
What you need 
 
 An EVM wallet: MetaMask, Rabby, Frame, Rainbow, or anything that speaks WalletConnect. 
 USDC on Hyperliquid to fund your trading balance. 
 

 1. Connect 
 Go to papertrade.xyz and click Connect . Your wallet pops once for a signature that registers a session key : a scoped keypair that signs your trades on your behalf for a window of time. After that single signature you won't see another wallet popup for normal trading. 

 2. Deposit 
 Click Deposit . The app shows you a unique deposit address: yours alone, deterministic, no one else's USDC will ever land there. Send any amount of USDC from any wallet. Within a few seconds it appears in your Papertrade trading balance. See Deposits and withdrawals for more. 

 3. Trade 
 Pick a market, a direction (long or short), how much margin to commit, and a leverage up to 1000×. Click Buy or Sell . The protocol enters you immediately at Hyperliquid's BBO mid. Close any time; the protocol reads the current mid and settles your PnL against the LP. There is no gas fee on the user side and no popup per trade; the relayer covers gas and the session key signs. 

 Next 
 
 Wins and losses : what you keep, what the protocol takes. 
 The LP and the payout queue : what you're trading against. 
 Paper Emissions : why you receive PAPER on losses.

learn/trades-pricing.title: Trades and pricing
learn/trades-pricing.lead: What a trade looks like from the trader's side, and where the price comes from.
learn/trades-pricing.text:
To open a trade, you pick a market (BTC or ETH for now), pick a direction (long or short), pick how much margin you want to commit and how much leverage you want on top, and click. The protocol opens the position immediately at Hyperliquid's order-book mid price. Closing works the same way: you click, the protocol reads the current mid, and your PnL settles against the LP. 

 Who you're trading against 
 The counterparty on every trade is the LP. There is no orderbook on Papertrade, no matching engine, no other trader on the other side. Whether you win or lose flows directly to or from the LP's balance. This is what lets the protocol skip slippage and funding costs entirely. 

 Where the price comes from 
 The price you trade at is Hyperliquid's order-book mid for that asset, read directly by the smart contract from Hyperliquid's network. There's no separate price feed, no oracle committee, no admin signer. The price the contract sees is the same price Hyperliquid's market makers are quoting at that block. 

 Fees, funding, slippage 
 No funding cost, no spread, and no user-paid gas. The relayer pays gas. The protocol economics are the asymmetric impact on profitable closes plus LP-side fee carves on solvent settlements; losses are not charged above the loss itself. 

 Margin 
 Each trade lives as its own self-contained position. The margin you commit at open is the margin that position carries until it ends. You cannot top it up to push back a liquidation, and you cannot pull margin out to free up collateral elsewhere. There's no cross-margining between positions, no isolated-vs-cross toggle, no leverage adjustment after the fact. 
 The only way to edit a position is to close it (you decide when, full size only) or have it liquidated (the protocol decides when, by hitting your bust price). Want to scale into the same direction? Open a second position. Want to take some risk off the table? Close this one and open a smaller one. 

 What's available, what's the cap 
 BTC and ETH today, both with up to 1000× leverage . Per-user position cap: $10M . Markets are added by the contract owner and are limited to assets that exist on Hyperliquid's order book.

learn/wins-losses.title: Wins and losses
learn/wins-losses.lead: What happens at close: what you keep, what the protocol takes, and what you receive on losses.
learn/wins-losses.text:
Winning closes 
 Your raw gain is the price move multiplied by your position notional. Before the protocol credits the gain to your account, it applies a small asymmetric impact : a smooth haircut that scales with how far price moved between entry and exit. Bigger moves keep more of the raw gain. Tiny moves are scaled the most. 
 This is the only thing the protocol takes from your trade. It's not a percentage fee on notional, and it's not a spread on the price you see. It's a scale factor applied to the realised PnL, and it only ever applies to gains. 

 
 
 

 Losing closes 
 Your raw loss is the price move multiplied by your position notional. Nothing extra is taken from you on top of that loss. When the payout queue is empty, the LP-side fee carve comes out of the LP's gain from the loss; when the queue is active, the loss parks in sideBucket and the fee is waived. 
 You also receive PAPER tokens for the realised loss. The amount depends on where tracked LP is on its emissions curve : the lower the LP, the more PAPER you mint per dollar of eligible loss basis. Insolvent losses still mint PAPER even when their cash is parked for queue harvest instead of immediately credited to LP. 

 Why it's called asymmetric 
 Wins are scaled (a haircut). Losses pay the full PnL but face no scaling on top. The cost of trading lives entirely on the win side, scaled by how much you actually won. 

 For the exact mechanics see Asymmetric impact PnL .

learn/liquidations.title: Liquidations
learn/liquidations.lead: How the displayed bust trigger differs from a voluntary close, and what a hard liquidation means.
learn/liquidations.text:
Every position has a displayed bust price . It is the hard-liquidation trigger, not a promise that the voluntary close path has already reduced the position's remaining equity to zero. Liquidation is a hard bust: crossing the displayed bust price forfeits the full isolated margin, even if a voluntary close immediately beforehand could return some equity. 

 The buffer 
 The trigger is a touch closer to your entry than the zero-equity price used as its reference point. The gap is a small fixed buffer baked into the contract, currently about 5 basis points (0.05% of price). Because crossing the trigger invokes the separate full-margin liquidation rule, that apparently small price gap can represent meaningful remaining close-path equity at high leverage. 
 A worked example: a $100 long opened at 100× leverage. A 1% drop — to $99 — would consume your full margin exactly. The protocol trips liquidation a little earlier, at roughly $99.05 . That last 0.05% is the buffer. 
 The shape is the same at lower leverage. At 10×, the threshold moves from 10% to about 9.95%. At 2×, from 50% to about 49.95%. The absolute offset stays around 5 basis points regardless of leverage. 
 The buffer exists so the LP is never on the wrong side of a liquidation. Prices can drift during the round-trip a keeper takes to land its transaction; the buffer is the cushion that ensures the LP captures the full position size before the close, even on fast moves. 

 When liquidation fires 
 If the BBO mid crosses your bust price, anyone running a liquidation keeper script can call the contract to liquidate your position. Liquidation does not settle the position as a voluntary close at the trigger price: it removes the position under the hard-bust path and forfeits the full isolated margin. 
 You lose the full isolated margin; that's what hard bust means. The contract routes that value through the applicable LP or queue accounting. You also receive PAPER for the lost margin, the same way you do on a regular losing close. 

 Who runs the keepers 
 Anyone can. The liquidation function is permissionless; the contract has no concept of "the official liquidator." The Papertrade team operates a keeper of its own, but no one is locked out of the role.

learn/lp-queue.title: The LP and the payout queue
learn/lp-queue.lead: What you're trading against, where its money comes from, and what happens when it can't pay out a winner immediately.
learn/lp-queue.text:
The LP 
 The LP is the protocol's balance of USDC held to settle trades. It starts at $0 . There is no seed capital, no founders' deposit, no upfront LP raise. The LP grows over time from cumulative user losses. 
 There is also no way for anyone to deposit directly into the LP. The only way to get exposure to LP economics is to hold or stake PAPER , the protocol's native token, which is minted to traders against losing closes and liquidations. In the relayer-only launch profile, PAPER cannot be freely transferred between wallets; staking and unstaking remain supported. 

 The payout queue 
 Sometimes the LP doesn't have enough USDC to immediately pay a winning close in full. When that happens, the unpaid portion of the win goes into a FIFO queue. The contract keeps a running list of unpaid wins and pays them out from the front as future losses (or future wins under the right conditions) refill the LP. 

 Your margin is never queued. When you close, the contract returns your original collateral to your balance instantly — only the profit portion of a winning close can land in the queue if the LP is short. On a losing close the loss comes out of your margin and the remainder is yours immediately. Even when the queue has wait time, your principal is always under your own control. 

 
 
 

 What this means for you 
 If you close a winning trade and the LP can pay you immediately, you're paid immediately. If the LP can't, the queue absorbs the difference and pays you out as solvency returns. Your queued payout is real on-chain debt: not a refund, not a haircut, just a delay. 
 Trading while the LP is low or underwater is incentivised by the PAPER emissions curve : that's exactly when PAPER mints fastest, and the queue tends to be empty. 

 For the academic background on this mechanism see the Martingaler LP overview . For the on-chain implementation see Solvency model: three-bucket queue .

learn/paper-emissions.title: Paper Emissions
learn/paper-emissions.lead: Why PAPER exists, how you earn it, and why the rate is biggest at the start.
learn/paper-emissions.text:
A fair launch by construction 
 PAPER starts at zero supply . No pre-mint, no team allocation, no VC allocation, no airdrop, no vesting. Every token that will ever exist has to be minted through the emissions curve described below, and the only people who can trigger a mint are the traders who close at a loss or get liquidated. The supply is purely community-owned by definition. The launch profile restricts arbitrary secondary transfers while preserving stake/unstake movement. 

 Why PAPER exists 
 PAPER is the LP's fee-claim token. Staking it gives you a pro-rata share of the protocol's future revenue. There is no other path to LP exposure: minting PAPER is how the protocol bootstraps an LP without any upfront capital, by routing a token reward to the people who put money in (which, in this design, means the people who lose trades). 

 How you earn it 
 PAPER mints to your account whenever you close a trade at a loss or get liquidated. Nothing else mints PAPER. The amount minted scales with your eligible realised loss basis: bigger losses mint more PAPER. 

 When the rate is highest 
 The mint rate isn't fixed. It depends on where the LP is sitting: 
 
 While tracked LP is below $2M (including any time it's underwater), the rate is a flat 100 PAPER per $1 of eligible loss basis . 
 Above $2M, the rate decays smoothly as the LP grows. The further the LP gets, the less PAPER each new dollar of loss mints. 
 
 Early traders earn materially more PAPER per dollar lost than late traders. By design: early activity carries the most variance risk and is rewarded the most. 

 
 
 

 For the technical curve and exact formula see Mint curve .

learn/staking-dividends.title: Staking Dividends
learn/staking-dividends.lead: What you can do with PAPER once you have it: stake to earn USDC, continuously and instantly.
learn/staking-dividends.text:
Staking PAPER 
 Stake any amount of PAPER, any time. Stake and unstake are both instant : there is no cooldown, no lockup, no vesting. The moment your PAPER is staked, you start earning a pro-rata share of the protocol's USDC dividends. 

 Where the dividends come from 
 Two sources, both flowing from the LP to stakers continuously in USDC. The user pays nothing extra for either; both are cuts of the LP's revenue. 
 
 A share of LP revenue. Every settlement that credits the LP (the asymmetric impact taken from winning closes, plus the LP's gain on losing and liquidation closes) carves a small slice for stakers continuously. 
 An LP excess sweep. Once the LP grows past its $5M cap , every dollar of LP gain past that point is fully sweepable to stakers. Below $5M, only the LP-revenue share routes to stakers; above, the surplus routes too. 
 

 Claiming 
 Your accrued dividends sit in the staking contract until you claim. The frontend shows your accumulated balance live; you can claim at any time and the USDC moves to your trading balance. 

 For the on-chain mechanics see Staking & claims .

learn/deposits-withdrawals.title: Deposits and withdrawals
learn/deposits-withdrawals.lead: USDC moves into and out of Papertrade through a single per-user address. That address exists on both Hyperliquid layers, but only the HyperCore side is what the protocol watches; every supported deposit path ends there.
learn/deposits-withdrawals.text:
Your deposit address 
 When you connect your wallet, the app gives you a unique deposit address. That address is yours alone, derived deterministically from your wallet; nobody else's USDC can ever land there. 
 The same address exists on both HyperCore (Hyperliquid's native spot ledger) and HyperEVM (Hyperliquid's L1 EVM). Hyperliquid uses one address space across both layers, so the deposit address you copy is simultaneously a Core spot account and a HyperEVM contract (a per-user CREATE2 proxy that the protocol deploys on first use). 
 Papertrade only credits balance from the HyperCore side. USDC needs to arrive in the Core spot account at that deterministic address. The address is registered before dispatch; once funded, the settlement worker deploys the matching proxy if necessary and sweeps the Core balance into your Papertrade trading balance. 

 
 
 

 How to send USDC 
 From Hyperliquid spot. If you already hold USDC on your HL spot account, just transfer it directly to your deposit address on HL Core. This is the simplest path: one HL spot send, no bridge, and your balance lands in seconds. 
 From HyperEVM. The guided HL EVM route approves Circle's canonical native USDC and deposits it through the official CoreDepositWallet before the normal Papertrade proxy sweep. Do not send an arbitrary token with a USDC symbol: the contract address is verified exactly. 
 From Solana, Arbitrum, or Ethereum. Papertrade uses Circle CCTP V2 directly to HyperEVM domain 19. Circle's CctpForwarder deposits the net native USDC into your deterministic Papertrade proxy on HyperCore spot, and the existing request/finalize sweep credits your Exchange balance. Solana and Ethereum do not detour through Arbitrum, and no Hyperliquid signature is requested midway through settlement. 
 Every source authorization is completed before dispatch. The supported source assets are only canonical Circle USDC: Solana EPjF…Dt1v , Arbitrum 0xaf88…5831 , and Ethereum 0xA0b8…eB48 . A raw ERC-20 transfer to the proxy on HyperEVM is still not monitored; use the guided HL EVM route instead. 

 Withdrawing 
 You can withdraw any time, up to your available balance. Sign once; the Exchange sends USDC directly to your HL Core spot account at the same address. From there you can keep it on HL or bridge it out. Funds typically arrive in a few seconds. 
 Open positions are not withdrawable. Your available balance is what is not currently committed as margin. 

 Technical detail 
 For the proxy contract, CREATE2 derivation, sweeper, and CoreWriter mechanics see Deposits: CREATE2 proxies .

learn/session-keys.title: Session keys
learn/session-keys.lead: Why you don't get a wallet popup on every trade, and what's actually being authorised.
learn/session-keys.text:
Why one click is enough 
 When you first connect your wallet to Papertrade, the app asks you to sign a single message to register a session key . After that, your individual trades (opens, closes, staking actions) don't pop a wallet signature. The session key signs them on your behalf, scoped to your account, for a window of time, and the relayer/batcher submits the signed intents onchain. 

 What a session key can do 
 
 Open and close positions on your account. 
 Move funds between your trading balance and your positions. 
 Stake and unstake PAPER on your behalf. 
 

 What a session key cannot do 
 
 It cannot withdraw your funds to an external address. Withdrawals always require your real wallet's signature. 
 It cannot move PAPER off the contract. 
 
 Worst case if a session key is compromised: an attacker can place trades on your account but cannot steal your funds. You can revoke a session key from your wallet at any time. 

 Expiry 
 Session keys last seven days. Every trade a session key signs is valid for one hour, so the app asks you to sign a new session key once the current one has less than an hour left.

how/architecture.title: Architecture overview
how/architecture.lead: The protocol is a set of contracts on the HyperEVM L1 that uses Hyperliquid's HyperCore precompiles for pricing and bridging. This page maps the contracts and how they fit together.
how/architecture.text:
Contracts (HyperEVM) 
 
 Exchange : the main trading contract. Tracks user balances, opens and closes positions, settles PnL, manages the payout queue, holds the LP balance. The relayer-only launch profile gates trading entrypoints behind the batch executor while leaving withdrawals and maintenance paths separate. 
 BatchExecutor : entry contract for batched intents. In the launch profile, BatchExecutorRelayerOnly accepts batches only from configured relayer keys, then unpacks N user intents and dispatches them to Exchange . 
 PaperToken , PaperStaking , PaperTokenomics : the PAPER token, staking contract, and mint-rate calculator. The relayer-only launch profile uses a non-transferable PAPER token profile while preserving staking movement. 
 SessionKeyManager : registers and validates session keys, so a user can authorise a scoped key once and sign individual intents off-chain without a wallet popup. In the launch profile, registration is submitted through the authorised batch/relayer path; revocation remains a direct user action. 
 PriceOracle : wraps the BBO/Mark/Oracle precompiles for in-contract reads. 
 DepositProxyFactory + Create2DepositProxy : derive per-user deterministic deposit addresses; bridge incoming USDC from HyperCore into the Exchange. 
 

 Precompiles (HyperCore) 
 
 BBO 0x...080e : best-bid/ask read; the protocol's execution price. 
 Mark 0x...0806 : Hyperliquid's "fair" mark; read for analytics and future cross-checks. 
 Oracle 0x...0807 : validator-median external reference; read for forward-compat. 
 CoreWriter : the bridge interface. Used by Create2DepositProxy to push USDC from the user's proxy Core account into the Exchange's HyperCore account, and by Exchange.withdrawToCore to move funds back to the user's Core spot account. 
 

 A trade end-to-end 
 A signed user intent hits the relayer, then the authorised BatchExecutor , which unpacks it and calls Exchange.openPositionBySig (or close, staking, etc). Exchange reads the BBO precompile through PriceOracle for the execution price, settles PnL against the LP, updates the user's internal balance, and mints PAPER on realised losses through PaperTokenomics . Multiple users' intents can be batched into a single EVM transaction; each one is dispatched and settled independently inside BatchExecutor . 

 Frontends 
 The relayer-only launch profile intentionally makes the configured relayer/batcher the trading submitter. A different frontend can still produce compatible user signatures and integrate with that path, but it cannot bypass the authorised batch executor for opens/closes on the relayer-only deployment. The open and session-fee contract profiles keep the direct public submitter surface for future or alternate deployments.

how/pricing-bbo.title: Pricing: BBO precompile
how/pricing-bbo.lead: Papertrade reads prices directly from Hyperliquid's native order book via an EVM precompile. No off-chain oracle, no pricing bot, no admin key that can change what the market sees.
how/pricing-bbo.text:
BBO precompile technical implementation 
 A perps exchange needs a price feed for two things: executing new trades and marking open positions to compute PnL and liquidations. On most L1s this is a hard problem: you either trust a centralised oracle, run a decentralised one that's slow and expensive, or accept that a single operator can freeze the market by withholding updates. 
 Hyperliquid ships a way out. HyperCore (the consensus layer that runs HL's native spot and perp order books) is observable from the HyperEVM via L1 read precompiles : fixed-address system contracts that any EVM contract can staticcall to read live HyperCore state. Prices included. 
 We use one of them, the BBO precompile at 0x000000000000000000000000000000000000080e . Given a HyperCore asset index (on the current chain-999 deployment, BTC = 0 and ETH = 1 ), it returns the current best bid and best ask on HL's native book: 
 (bool ok, bytes memory result) = PRECOMPILE_BBO.staticcall(abi.encode(asset));
(uint64 bid, uint64 ask) = abi.decode(result, (uint64, uint64)); 
 Papertrade's execution price is simply the midpoint: 
 price = (bid + ask) / 2; 
 That's the whole pricing stack. 

 What this gives up, and what it gives us 
 The trade-off is honest: we can only list markets that already exist on HL's order book. You won't be able to trade something HL doesn't trade: no long-tail DeFi tokens or hypothetical RWAs, unless HL lists them first. 
 In return, we get a pricing pipeline with no centralised component at all. The BBO precompile is consensus-verified HyperCore state, same as the balances on HL's L1 bridge. No price signer, no oracle committee, no admin multisig that can point the oracle elsewhere. The price the exchange sees is the price HL's market makers are quoting at that block, readable by any contract, provable on-chain. 

 No deviation breaker 
 Someone can try to manipulate the HL order book for a block by widening the spread or moving the inside quote, then trade Papertrade against the distorted midpoint. That is a real protocol risk of using BBO directly. 
 PriceOracle reverts if the precompile returns zero or a crossed book ( ask < bid ), but it has no maximum-deviation, time-weighted-price, or lookback breaker. A non-zero, uncrossed but manipulated BBO can therefore be accepted for execution. The deadband and asymmetric-impact curve reduce some small-move payoffs, while configurable per-side OI caps limit additional exposure. They do not prove manipulation unprofitable or place a hard bound on protocol loss; see Risk . 

 The one centralised lever: pause-opens 
 There's exactly one admin action over pricing that runs in real time: pausing opens on a market . The pause guardian calls Exchange.pauseMarket(instrumentId) , which captures the current BBO into a frozen bid/ask pair and flips the pause flag. While paused: 
 
 New opens on that market revert with MarketPaused . 
 Closes and liquidations still succeed, but they read the frozen BBO instead of the live precompile. 
 
 The frozen price is what lets us pause without stranding open positions: a trader who opened before the pause can still get out at a price that made sense at the moment the operator intervened, even if HL's book has moved wildly since. The pause is scoped per-market, so a problem with one asset doesn't take the whole exchange down. There's also a global setTradingPaused(true) for the same guardian, used only as a kill switch in emergencies. 
 Everything else admin can do (tuning fee/impact params, adding markets, swapping keepers) is owner-only and runs at the cadence of normal contract ops.

how/deposits.title: Deposits: CREATE2 proxies
how/deposits.lead: Deposits work by sending USDC to a personal, per-user address. No approve popup, no signature, no on-chain transaction you have to send yourself. It's the same UX as a CEX deposit, built on top of entirely on-chain mechanics.
how/deposits.text:
Your own deposit address 
 Every user has a unique deposit address, computed deterministically from their wallet address using CREATE2. The address can be predicted before deployment; in the launch profile the relayer ensures the proxy contract is deployed before the address is used. 
 The UI shows you this address when you click Deposit . Hyperliquid spot sends and Circle CCTP bridge routes land on the HyperCore side of that address. The guided HL EVM route first moves canonical native USDC through CoreDepositWallet; a raw ERC-20 transfer to the proxy is not monitored. 

 The sweeper picks it up 
 A keeper daemon (the "sweeper") watches every deployed user's proxy address on HyperCore. When it sees a positive spot or withdrawable perp USDC balance, it drives the Exchange sweep flow: 
 
 requestSweep(user) : records the proxy's Core balances and calls the proxy to move spot/perp USDC into the Exchange's Core account. 
 finalizeSweep(user) : after the Core transfer clears, credits the user's internal Exchange balance. 
 
 The proxy calls HL's CoreWriter precompile under the hood. Funds usually land in your Papertrade balance within a few HL blocks, with the UI blocking rapid repeat deposits during the two-step sweep window. 
 The sweep/finalize Exchange calls are public maintenance paths, but proxy deployment is relayer-gated in the launch profile to avoid public gas griefing. The protocol team operates the sweeper for normal UX latency. 

 Why proxies, not direct deposits 
 Two reasons. First: UX. A direct deposit would require you to sign two transactions (the approval and the deposit) each with gas. Proxies turn the whole flow into a passive transfer you can do from literally any source. 
 Second: per-user isolation. Each user's proxy is a distinct address. Nobody else's balance can collide with yours, and the sweeper can reason about each user independently without global accounting. If the sweeper misbehaves for one user, the others are unaffected. 

 What you're trusting 
 The proxy contracts are deployed from a single DepositProxyFactory using CREATE2 with a fixed bytecode. Anyone can derive the expected proxy address for any wallet off-chain and verify the on-chain proxy matches: the factory, the salt, and the init code hash are all public. If the bytecode ever changes, the derived address changes; your old deposit address would become an empty slot and would not silently map to different code. 
 The proxy's sweep functions are onlyExchange -gated, so only the Exchange contract can trigger Core transfers out of the proxy. ERC-20 tokens accidentally sent to the HyperEVM proxy can be recovered by the proxy owner with withdrawStuckToken ; they are not counted as Papertrade deposits.

how/solvency-queue.title: Solvency & queue
how/solvency-queue.lead: Papertrade's LP can be temporarily insolvent. A FIFO payout queue and a parked-funds side bucket guarantee winners eventually get paid, in order, while keeping the protocol from blocking new trades.
how/solvency-queue.text:
The model 
 Conceptually, Papertrade has three separate accounting buckets: 
 
 treasury : the LP balance. Cannot go negative. 
 sideBucket : loss proceeds parked while the queue is non-empty. Drained first by harvest into queue payouts. 
 Payout queue : a FIFO of unpaid winning closes. Each entry: (user, amount) . 
 
 This is the Martingaler mechanism : instead of holding pre-funded LP that pays winners on demand, the protocol queues winners when reserves are short, and clears them as future losses replenish the LP. 

 What enters the queue and what doesn't. The queue holds only the profit portion of a winning close that exceeded the LP's available budget at close time . Several things explicitly stay out: 
 
 Margin / collateral on a USD-funded close — returned to balances[user] immediately via marginCredit (see QueueLib.settleUsd : marginOut = size256 ). The user can withdraw or reuse it without waiting on the queue. 
 Trade fees on insolvent closes — suppressed entirely while the queue is non-empty (no fee charged), so user value isn't siphoned during deficit. 
 Losses while queue non-empty — parked in sideBucket instead of being booked as immediate LP gain; harvest uses available queue-backing cash and debits sideBucket first. 
 

 
 
 Loss/liq proceeds route to treasury (queue empty) or sideBucket (queue active). Wins pay direct from treasury when solvent, else queue. Harvest pays queued claims from available backing cash and debits sideBucket first. 
 

 Winning closes 
 When a user closes at a profit: 
 
 If the queue is empty and treasury ≥ payout : pay the user immediately, debit treasury. 
 Otherwise: append (user, payout) to the back of the queue. Treasury is unchanged. 
 

 Losing closes & liquidations 
 When a user closes at a loss (or is liquidated): 
 
 If the queue is empty: the LP-retained slice (loss minus 2% fee) credits the treasury directly. 
 If the queue is non-empty: the loss proceeds are parked in sideBucket instead of treasury and the loss fee is waived. PAPER mint still fires for realised losses, including insolvent close losses and liquidations; the cash routing to sideBucket does not suppress PAPER emission. 
 

 Harvest 
 A keeper periodically calls harvest(maxEntries) : 
 
 Walk the queue head forward, paying out each entry (user, amount) from available queue-backing cash. 
 Debit sideBucket first for the amount paid. If available backing cash runs out before the queue is clear, stop. Future losses or freed cash can fund later harvests. 
 If the queue empties with sideBucket > 0 , the residual returns to treasury as normal LP gain. 
 
 Harvest is permissionless; anyone can run it. The pt-harvester keeper does it on a schedule so users don't have to. 

 Invariants 
 
 treasury ≥ 0 by type and by construction (uint128). 
 sideBucket ≥ 0 by construction. 
 Net protocol equity = treasury + sideBucket − queueTotal . This can go negative ; that's the Martingaler "temporary insolvency" by design. 
 

 What the user sees 
 Opening a position is unaffected by queue state except for normal OI caps and debt-queue gas limits. Closing at a profit may either pay you directly or queue you, depending on solvency. The UI shows both an "available" balance (paid out) and a "queued" balance (waiting on harvest); both are spendable for new opens, because queued balance can be consumed as position collateral. 
 Source: contracts/src/QueueLib.sol and the close/liquidate flows in contracts/src/Exchange.sol .

how/asymmetric-impact.title: Asymmetric impact PnL
how/asymmetric-impact.lead: How Papertrade settles closing PnL, the only thing the protocol takes from a trade.
how/asymmetric-impact.text:
Trades enter at BBO mid , and a later close uses the BBO mid at the block in which that close executes. There is no spread, no slippage, no funding, no notional trading fee, and no gas charged to the user. Losses are not charged above the loss itself; in solvent cases the LP-side loss fee is carved from the LP's gain, and in insolvent cases it is waived. 
 On profitable closes , the protocol applies an asymmetric-impact haircut to the resulting PnL. It is not a percentage fee on notional or a spread on the execution price: it multiplies the raw gain by a scale factor determined by the entry-to-exit move. The haircut can consume most of a very small gain and becomes less severe as the move grows. 

 Properties 
 
 Asymmetric. Only winning closes are scaled. Losing closes pay nothing extra. 
 Move-sized, not position-sized. The haircut percentage doesn't depend on whether you're closing $100 or $100K of notional. A reference notional set per market controls the steepness; the size of your trade does not. 
 Bigger moves keep more of the gain. The haircut shrinks smoothly as the move grows. Tiny moves are scaled the most aggressively; larger moves keep most of the raw gain. 
 

 The formula 
 For a winning close, the protocol applies a scale factor to the raw PnL: 
 adjustedPnl = rawPnl × scale
scale = (1 − baseRate) / (1 + term1 + term2)
term1 = 1 / (move × rateMultiplier)
term2 = referenceNotional / (move × positionMultiplier)
move = |exitPrice − entryPrice| / entryPrice 
 baseRate , rateMultiplier , positionMultiplier , and referenceNotional are per-instrument governance knobs. As move grows, both term1 and term2 shrink, the denominator approaches 1, and the trader keeps a larger share of rawPnl . As move approaches zero, the terms blow up and the scaled gain collapses toward zero. The exact implementation lives in QueueLib.applyMarketImpact . 

 Why term2 is fixed 
 In Rollbit's original formulation, term2 scales with the actual position notional, so the haircut percentage grows with trade size. We can't carry that property at 1000× leverage: it would push traders toward many small positions (more trades, more state, more gas) without making the per-trade economics any better for anyone. Papertrade substitutes a per-instrument referenceNotional constant for the position size in term2 . The curve is otherwise sound; the haircut percentage is now identical for a $100 close and a $100K close. 

 Why this design 
 At 1000× leverage, no fee on notional and no spread on price could plausibly sustain the LP: each one would either be invisible to the protocol or impossible for the user to bear. The asymmetric impact moves the cost into the only place that scales with realised outcome: the user's gain on a successful trade. Losses never pay extra. 
 The curve also adds economic friction to small gains, including gains that may come from briefly distorting BBO. It is not a deviation check, however, and does not guarantee that a manipulation strategy is unprofitable. Papertrade accepts that residual risk when it reads BBO without a breaker; see No deviation breaker . 

 Inspiration 
 The mechanism is adapted from Rollbit's market-impact model, which uses a similar PnL-side haircut to fund their LP without a traditional spread. Papertrade's variant fixes the position-size factor to a per-market reference notional, so the haircut percentage doesn't depend on how big a position you take.

how/builder-codes.title: Builder codes
how/builder-codes.lead: A planned 1% revenue share for frontends that originate trades. Not yet live.
how/builder-codes.text:
Coming soon 
 Builder codes are not yet live. This page describes the planned mechanism so integrators can see the shape of what's coming. 
 

 Builder codes will let any frontend earn a share of revenue from trades it originates. The model follows Hyperliquid's native builder-code design: a frontend tags its intents with a builder identifier, and when the trade settles the protocol routes 1% of the LP-revenue carve to the builder's address. 

 No impact on the user 
 Builder codes do not change anything the user pays. The 1% comes from the LP-revenue carve, the same source that funds staker dividends . There is no additional fee on top of the user's trade. From the user's perspective, builder codes are invisible. 

 Who can register 
 Anyone running a frontend that drives volume to Papertrade, once this profile is enabled. The relayer-only launch path still controls which submitters can reach the batch executor; permissionless builder-code routing is future-facing and depends on the matching open/session-fee deployment profile. 

 papertrade.xyz is the first canonical frontend 
 papertrade.xyz is the canonical implementation operated by the protocol team. On the relayer-only launch profile, the protocol's relayer/batcher is explicitly privileged as the trading submitter. 
 Permissionless builder codes are coming soon. Once the on-chain plumbing is finalised, any frontend will be able to register, tag its intents with a builder identifier, and earn the 1% revenue share on the volume it brings in. 

 When 
 No firm date. We will document the registration flow, the per-intent tagging surface, and the builder-payout claim mechanics here once the on-chain plumbing is finalised.

how/risk.title: Risk
how/risk.lead: The main protocol-level risk surface is BBO price manipulation on Hyperliquid's order book. This page covers that unresolved vector, the contract's economic frictions and exposure controls, the operational guards on top, and the gated/public/admin surfaces.
how/risk.text:
BBO jitter risk 
 Papertrade reads its execution price directly from Hyperliquid's BBO. The natural BBO spread on BTC and ETH is tight but non-zero, and within that spread an attacker can place a small limit order on HL's book that does not need to fill: simply sitting on the inside changes the best bid or best ask, which moves the BBO mid by a tick or two. 
 An attacker who shifts BBO this way may be able to open or close a Papertrade position at a distorted midpoint and profit when the quote returns toward the natural market. This is a real residual risk: the pricing pipeline has no independent reference price against which to reject the quote. 

 Economic frictions and exposure controls 
 The protocol has three relevant controls, but none is proof that BBO manipulation is impossible or unprofitable: 
 
 0.2 bps jitter-protection deadband. On a winning close, raw profit smaller than entryPrice / 50000 (≈0.2 bps of price) is zeroed before the impact curve runs; larger wins have that amount removed before scaling. 
 Asymmetric impact curve. The haircut on profitable closes is steepest on the smallest moves, reducing the payout from some small BBO distortions without comparing BBO to an independent price. 
 Configurable directional OI caps. Every instrument has independent long and short caps, and an open that would exceed the selected side's cap reverts. Under the keeper's default policy, each side targets its current OI plus asset quantity worth $5M at the current BBO. The keeper leaves the cap alone while that headroom remains within a 10% hysteresis band ($4.5M–$5.5M at the default) and rebuilds it toward $5M outside the band. These are limits on new per-side exposure, not a $5M total-OI ceiling, a loss ceiling, or a guarantee against manipulation profit. 
 
 Together these controls can reduce payoff and limit how much new directional exposure fits under the configured caps. A manipulated but non-zero, uncrossed BBO can still pass the oracle, so residual manipulation and LP-loss risk remain. 

 Operational guards 
 
 Rigorous watching keeper set. The protocol team operates an active keeper set that monitors BBO, open interest, and live position health, and runs the permissionless harvest and liquidation paths. None of these roles are exclusive: harvest and liquidations are open, so any third party can run their own keeper alongside the protocol's. 
 Terminal market retirement and global opens gate. The pause guardian can retire a market ID if something looks anomalous; that ID can never accept another open, and existing positions remain closeable only against the BBO frozen at retirement. The product may later be listed again under a fresh instrument ID. The separate global trading pause is the reversible way to halt opens without retiring markets. 
 Trailing OI cap operator. The market keeper applies the configured policy independently to each side. With the defaults it targets current OI plus $5M of BBO-valued headroom and updates only after that headroom leaves the 10% hysteresis band. 
 

 Permissionless and gated surfaces 
 The relayer-only launch profile gates trading submission through configured relayer keys: opens, closes, session-key registration, proxy deployment, and staking actions are submitted through the authorised batch/executor path. This is a launch hardening choice, not a signature model change: user intents are still signed by the user's wallet/session key and checked onchain. 
 Withdrawals remain user-controlled: direct withdrawToCore is callable by the wallet, and withdrawToCoreBySig can be submitted by anyone but requires the user's real wallet signature. Liquidations, queue harvest, sweep/finalize maintenance, and pushing Exchange-held staker fees remain public maintenance paths. The contract has no admin kill-switch on user balances; user value can be in available balance, open-position margin, or queued debt collateral. 

 Admin keys 
 Three roles, each scoped to a narrow surface: 
 
 Pause guardian. Can retire an instrument ID or engage the reversible global opens gate. Market retirement freezes the oracle : the BBO snapshot captured at retirement becomes the permanent close price for that ID. The retired ID cannot be unpaused or reopened; a later relist uses a fresh instrument ID. Existing positions remain closeable against the frozen BBO. 
 Owner. Holds contract ownership and proxy-admin control behind the governance timelock. Through it the owner can tune impact-curve and fee-rate parameters, claim accumulated dev fees, swap configured relayers/keepers, list new markets, reconcile orphaned deposits, and ultimately upgrade the contract implementation. The contracts are proxied, so in principle the owner can do anything the implementation can be rewritten to do; the timelock is what makes that visible before execution. 
 Market keeper. Moves the configurable per-asset, per-side OI caps. Can effectively pause new opens on a side by setting its cap to zero, but unlike the pause guardian this does not freeze the oracle: the BBO still floats and closes still settle at live BBO mid. Cannot move user collateral, cannot freeze the oracle, and cannot touch the impact curve.

paper/overview.title: $PAPER overview
paper/overview.lead: $PAPER is Papertrade's native token. It captures a share of LP revenue when staked and is minted to traders against losing closes and liquidations.
paper/overview.text:
What $PAPER is 
 $PAPER is an ERC-20-style token with two roles. The relayer-only launch profile restricts arbitrary transfers, but minting, staking, unstaking, and claims still work through the protocol path. 
 
 LP-revenue share. Staked $PAPER earns a pro-rata claim on the LP's revenue, distributed continuously in USDC. The user pays nothing extra for this; it is a cut of the LP's revenue, not an additional fee on the trade. 
 Loss-backed supply. $PAPER is minted to a trader when they realise an eligible loss (closing at a loss or being liquidated) as a consolation claim on future protocol value. 
 

 Fair launch 
 $PAPER is a fair launch in the strictest sense. Supply starts at zero . No pre-mint, no team allocation, no VC allocation, no airdrop, no vesting schedule. Every token that will ever exist must be minted through the on-chain emissions curve, and the only people who can trigger a mint are traders who close at a loss or get liquidated. The supply is purely community-owned by definition: anyone who wants exposure has to participate. 

 How supply grows 
 Supply expands purely from trading activity. The mint curve is front-loaded: while tracked LP is below the $2M flat threshold (including underwater), every $1 of eligible loss mint basis mints 100 PAPER . Above that threshold, the rate decays asymptotically as cumulative LP gain grows. 

 What stakers earn 
 Two revenue streams route from the LP to staked PAPER. Both are LP-side carves; the user pays nothing extra for either. 
 
 LP-revenue share. Every settlement that credits the LP (the asymmetric impact on winning closes, plus the LP's gain on losing and liquidation closes) carves a small slice for stakers continuously. 
 LP excess sweep. Once the LP balance climbs above the $5M staker reward cap , every dollar of further LP gain past that point is fully distributable to stakers via the public pushStakerFees() call. 
 
 Both streams pay out as USDC, claimable through the staking flow. In the relayer-only launch profile, claim submission goes through the authorised executor path. 

 Contracts 
 See PAPER contracts for the on-chain addresses of PaperToken , PaperStaking , and PaperTokenomics .

how/mint-curve.title: PAPER mint curve
how/mint-curve.lead: The flat-then-ratchet curve that turns realised loss basis into PAPER supply. Early activity mints at a constant rate while tracked LP is underwater or small; later activity mints asymptotically less.
how/mint-curve.text:
The shape 
 The curve has two regions, parametrised by four constants in PaperTokenomics : 
 
 Flat region (when trackedLpUsd < lpFlatThresholdUsd , including negative): mint rate is the constant flatRate = 100 PAPER per $1 of mint basis . The mint basis is the user's eligible realised loss, not necessarily the cash that immediately credited LP. 
 Ratchet region (when trackedLpUsd ≥ lpFlatThresholdUsd ): rate decays as the high-water-mark of cumulative LP gain past the threshold ( tailProgressUsd ) grows. The closed-form rate at HWM H is flatRate · (S / (S + H))² where S = tailDecayScaleUsd . 
 
 Live defaults: lpFlatThresholdUsd = $2M , flatRate = 100 , tailDecayScaleUsd = $120M . 

 
 
 
 Marginal mint rate vs tracked LP, with defaults flatRate=100 , threshold=$2M , S=$120M .
 Insolvent region (tracked LP < 0) and flat region both mint at the full 100 PAPER/$ of eligible loss basis; the tail decays as 100 · (S/(S+H))² where H = tailProgressUsd .
 
 

 Strict-monotone ratchet (v2) 
 tailProgressUsd is a strict high-water-mark: staker drains debit trackedLpUsd but do not reduce tailProgressUsd . Once the cumulative tail-region gain has advanced, the rate is permanently decayed by that amount. Concrete consequence: cumulative tail-region losses of $100M ⇒ HWM stays at $100M ⇒ the rate is now 100 · (120/220)² ≈ 30 PAPER/$ regardless of how often the LP got drained to stakers in between. 
 Early traders mint at materially higher rates than late traders. By design. 

 What counts as "loss" 
 The mint basis is the user's eligible realised loss after any LP-side loss-fee carve. On a solvent loss close the 2% loss-branch fee is carved from LP's side, so PAPER mints on rawLoss − fee while tracked LP also advances by that credited amount. On an insolvent close, no fee is taken, the loss can park in sideBucket , and PAPER still mints on the realised loss basis even though trackedLpUsd is not inflated by the sideBucket park. Liquidations mint on the lost margin in full, regardless of solvency state. Debt-funded losses mint on the destroyed portion of the user's queue claim.

paper/staking.title: Staking & claims
paper/staking.lead: Stake PAPER, earn a pro-rata share of LP revenue in USDC. Stake and unstake are both instant: no cooldown, no lockup.
paper/staking.text:
Stake 
 In the normal app flow, stake through the session-key route. Your stake earns fees continuously from the moment it's deposited. No vesting, no minimum. 
 In the open contract profile this maps to PaperStaking.stake(amount) or stakeBySig . In the relayer-only launch profile, direct public staking calls are disabled and stakeBySig is submitted by the authorised executor. The PAPER token auto-approves the staking contract, so the user does not need a separate approval transaction. 

 Unstake 
 Unstake through the same staking flow. Your PAPER returns to your wallet balance immediately, your stake stops earning fees, and any USDC rewards already accrued remain claimable. There is no cooldown . In the relayer-only launch profile the submitted function is unstakeBySig through the authorised executor. 

 Claims 
 Trading-fee revenue accrues as a per-stake claimable USDC balance via the global accRewardPerShare accumulator. Claim any time through the app; the claim credits your USDC balance on the Exchange contract, and from there you can withdraw to HyperCore. In the relayer-only launch profile this is claimBySig through the authorised executor. 
 Want to know your unclaimed balance without spending gas? Read PaperStaking.pendingReward(addr) . 

 How rewards arrive 
 Fee revenue lives in two places until distributed: 
 
 The Exchange's stakerFeeAccumulator collects the staker share of every trade fee. Anyone can call Exchange.pushStakerFees() to forward the accumulated balance to PaperStaking. 
 Once received by PaperStaking, distribution updates the global accRewardPerShare so all stakers' pending rewards advance pro-rata. In the relayer-only launch profile, direct public distribute() is disabled and the executor uses the signed distribution path. 
 
 The pt-fee-claimer keeper daemon does this on a schedule so users don't have to think about it. 

 The math 
 Reward share is strictly proportional to your staked balance divided by the global staked total, integrated over the period you held that stake. There are no boosts, no lockups, no tiers. A dollar of PAPER staked for an hour earns exactly what any other dollar staked for the same hour did.

dev/contract-addresses.title: Contract addresses
dev/contract-addresses.lead: Canonical contract addresses for the active deployment.
dev/contract-addresses.text:
The published runtime deployment descriptor is the canonical source for the active chain, contracts, and instruments. The browser release embeds its exact deployment fingerprint at build time. 
 The full deployment record is audit evidence, not a browser or service configuration API. The relayer-only, open, and session-fee contract profiles share most interfaces but differ in submitter permissions and PAPER transfer/staking rules.

 Key user-facing functions
